guidance.procedure: Use Contradiction only when an operative clause affirmatively conflicts with the exact proposition; silence, a different restriction, or merely related language is NotMentioned. Match actor, action, object, modality, quantifier, trigger, and exception. Example: a ban on disclosure does not oppose or establish a ban on reverse engineering; absent reverse-engineering language, that proposition remains unresolved.

operations.rationale: Across the batch, absent reverse-engineering terms were repeatedly labeled Contradiction using unrelated clauses, and several other errors likewise substituted topical proximity for exact opposition.

guidance.procedure: Select every sparse, independently responsive member required by the annotation structure. When an operative subparagraph depends on a governing lead-in such as an exclusion, permission, undertaking, or definition, include both the lead-in and the responsive item. Include separately operative repetitions, but exclude headings, neighboring context, and clauses that merely share a topic. Never substitute a convenient nearby clause for the clause supporting the stated reason.

operations.rationale: Most correct relations still missed governing introductions, repeated provisions, or operative companion clauses, while several answers cited headings or unrelated nearby text.

guidance.procedure: A no-reverse-engineering proposition requires an operative prohibition on reverse engineering, decompiling, disassembling, testing, analyzing, or an expressly equivalent treatment of an object embodying confidential information. A confidentiality, nondisclosure, limited-use, marking, or representative-access clause alone is unresolved, not opposing. Cite only the actual engineering restriction when present; otherwise use no evidence.

operations.rationale: Seven of eight answers used unrelated evidence and treated the absence of reverse-engineering language as Contradiction.

guidance.procedure: For destruction or return upon termination, verify both the disposition duty and its trigger. A clause triggered only by demand or request does not establish a termination-triggered duty. A duty triggered by termination, cessation of service, or the specified end or failure of the contemplated relationship can support it. Include the complete clause expressing both trigger and required disposition; do not infer the trigger from survival or general term language.

operations.rationale: The lawyer repeatedly treated demand-based return provisions as termination provisions and sometimes cited an unrelated survival clause.

guidance.procedure: Post-return possession is supported only by an express retention allowance or exception, such as retained backups, archival copies, compliance records, or permitted residual material. A command to return or destroy all information, especially with a no-retention term, opposes the proposition. A choice between return and destruction does not itself permit retention. General ownership, mental impressions, or silence is not a substitute for an operative retention allowance.

operations.rationale: One answer converted authorization to destroy into permission to retain, while other answers blurred complete-disposition duties and genuine backup exceptions.

guidance.procedure: Read a nondisclosure rule together with its exceptions. Pattern: “do not disclose to representatives unless they need it for the stated purpose” affirmatively permits the qualifying disclosure; it does not contradict a proposition that some disclosure is allowed. For employee sharing, confirm employees are named or included in a defined representative class. For broader third-party sharing, employees alone are insufficient; look for consultants, agents, advisers, contractors, affiliates, or another qualifying nonparty class.

operations.rationale: Conditional representative and employee permissions were repeatedly mislabeled as contradictions, while employee-only provisions were sometimes overextended to consultants or advisers.

guidance.procedure: Decide whether the operative definition confines Confidential Information to technical subject matter. A definition expressly covering commercial, financial, personnel, contractual, marketing, business, or similarly nontechnical material opposes “only technical”; cite the defining introduction and each annotated nontechnical category rather than a heading. A definition expressly limited to technical information supports it. A generic reference to information without a clear subject-matter boundary may leave the proposition unresolved.

operations.rationale: The lawyer frequently reached the right broad-definition relation but omitted most annotated nontechnical members, and sometimes relied on fragments that did not establish the scope.

guidance.procedure: “All Confidential Information must be expressly identified” is supported when the definition or operative conditions require every covered form to be marked, designated, or identified, including any special procedure for oral disclosures. It is opposed when information qualifies regardless of labeling or through an objective reasonable-understanding standard. If only one subset must be marked while other information qualifies without identification, do not generalize the subset rule to all information.

operations.rationale: Observed errors confused broad confidentiality definitions with identification requirements and omitted the full multi-step marking procedure where it governed all covered forms.

guidance.procedure: Support verbal inclusion when the operative definition expressly names oral, spoken, or verbal disclosure, or clearly makes all forms covered in a way that includes oral disclosure. Employee-sharing provisions and broad subject-matter lists do not establish the medium. A clause addressing later oral communication is not necessarily a definition of Confidential Information. Select the defining clause and any dependent oral-identification conditions, not unrelated access terms.

operations.rationale: The lawyer inferred oral coverage from employee disclosure and from an unrelated broad list, and often omitted dependent oral-identification members.

guidance.procedure: Keep the two exception paths distinct. Independent-development support requires development without use of, reference to, or access to protected information. Third-party-acquisition support requires receipt from an outside source entitled to disclose and not bound by the relevant confidentiality restriction. Prior possession, compelled disclosure, or the other exception path does not prove the queried path. Include the governing exclusion lead-in plus the exact responsive item when the item depends on it.

operations.rationale: Answers repeatedly mixed prior possession, independent development, third-party receipt, and compelled disclosure, producing extra evidence and missing governing lead-ins.

guidance.procedure: A compelled-disclosure exception supports the notice proposition only if the recipient must notify, advise, or give the discloser an opportunity to object when disclosure is legally required. Permission or obligation to comply with law alone is insufficient. Include the governing compelled-disclosure or exclusion introduction and each operative notice provision, including separately applicable notification routes; omit generic disclosure restrictions.

operations.rationale: Relations were usually correct, but evidence systematically omitted governing introductions and additional operative notice provisions.

guidance.procedure: Support survival when a clause expressly says duties survive termination, continue beyond the term, or remain effective after the relevant relationship ends. A duration measured only from execution or receipt does not by itself establish survival; nor does a return clause. Include each independently operative survival statement and the provision identifying the surviving duty when annotated. Do not convert an agreement’s ordinary fixed term into post-termination survival.

operations.rationale: The lawyer inferred survival from fixed-duration and return clauses, missed explicit survival language, and added nonresponsive disposition evidence.

guidance.procedure: A qualified prohibition can create permission: “do not copy except as necessary for the stated purpose” supports permission to make some copies in that circumstance. An unqualified no-copy duty opposes it. Mere references to existing copies, return of copies, electronic storage, or documents prepared by the recipient do not alone authorize creation. Include the governing undertaking lead-in when the copying subparagraph depends on it.

operations.rationale: The lawyer sometimes missed the permission created by an express necessity exception and elsewhere used unrelated clauses instead of the operative copying rule.

guidance.procedure: For no grant of rights, distinguish ownership from an operative no-license or no-rights clause. Support comes from language denying licenses, title, use rights, intellectual-property rights, or other interests, subject to any expressly limited permitted use. Include separately operative no-grant provisions and their governing introduction; do not cite unrelated no-transaction, no-disclosure, or property-return clauses merely because they concern rights or ownership.

operations.rationale: Labels were stable, but evidence frequently omitted multiple annotated no-grant provisions or substituted unrelated ownership and transaction clauses.

guidance.procedure: Look specifically for confidentiality of the agreement’s existence or terms, or the fact, content, status, or terms of negotiations. A general duty protecting exchanged information does not settle this proposition. If the agreement or discussions are included through a definition, include the governing definition introduction together with the specific inclusion; if an operative nondisclosure clause directly covers them, select that clause.

operations.rationale: The principal missed evidence was the governing definition language needed to connect agreement and negotiation facts to protected information.

guidance.procedure: Support limited use when an operative duty confines use to the agreement’s stated purpose, whether phrased positively as “only for” or negatively as “not for any other purpose.” Include the governing undertaking or limited-purpose provision when the operative subparagraph depends on it, plus independently responsive repeated restrictions. Do not add disclosure, copying, implied-license, harm-recital, or authorization clauses unless they themselves impose the queried use limitation.

operations.rationale: Relations were correct, but evidence often omitted governing clauses and repeated use restrictions while adding disclosure, copying, or recital language.
